title: Impersonal Constructions
summary: Sentences with no subject at all: the weather, how a person feels, what hurts, and what is permitted. Lithuanian says these with a special form of the adjective that agrees with nothing, and with the dative already met at ¶69.

rules.heading: The Non-Gendered Adjective
rules.statement: Beside its masculine and feminine forms every qualitative adjective has a third, **non-gendered** form — the *negimininė forma*. It is made from the masculine by changing **-as** to **-a** and **-us** to **-u**, and it agrees with **nothing**, because in these sentences there is nothing for it to agree with. It is the form used when a state is reported without any person or thing being said to be in it.

paradigms.caption: The three forms of the adjective
paradigms.footnote: For adjectives in **-as** the non-gendered form is spelt like the feminine, and only the sentence tells them apart. For those in **-us** the two are distinct — *įdomi* against *įdomu* — and the difference is plain to see.

rules.heading: Personal against Impersonal
rules.statement: This is the distinction on which the whole section turns. **Filmas įdomus** says that the film *is* interesting — a subject, and an adjective agreeing with it. **Man įdomu** says that *I find it* interesting — no subject, the person in the **dative**, and the non-gendered form. English uses the same word for both and gives no warning; Lithuanian keeps them wholly apart.

paradigms.caption: Two sentences that English confuses
paradigms.footnote: *Ji šalta* and *jai šalta* differ by two letters and mean quite different things — the first describes what she is like, the second what she feels. It is worth reading the pair aloud until the difference is automatic.

examples.gloss: We had a very good time.
examples.note: the past of *būti* carries the impersonal sentence into the past

rules.heading: The Weather
rules.statement: The weather is reported either with a non-gendered adjective — *šalta*, *šilta*, *karšta* — or with a verb that has **no subject and never will have one**. *Lyja* is *it is raining*; there is no word answering to the English *it*, and supplying one is wrong. These verbs exist only in the third person.

examples.note: the past of an impersonal verb, still third person

rules.heading: What Hurts: Skaudėti
rules.statement: **Skaudėti** is impersonal and takes two things: the sufferer in the **dative**, and the part that hurts in the **accusative**. English makes the part the subject — *my head aches* — and Lithuanian makes it the object of a verb with no subject at all. This is the sentence a learner needs at the doctor's, and it is worth learning whole.
footnotes: Do not say *mano galva skauda*: the possessive and the nominative both belong to the English construction, not the Lithuanian one.

rules.heading: What Is Necessary and What Is Allowed
rules.statement: **Reikia** was given at ¶69; it is one of a small family. **Galima** is *it is possible, one may*; **negalima** is *it is forbidden*; **verta** is *it is worth while*. All are impersonal, all are completed by an **infinitive**, and all take the person concerned in the **dative** if he is mentioned at all. Because they are impersonal they have no personal endings — they change only for tense.

paradigms.caption: The impersonals and their tenses
paradigms.footnote: *Galima* is itself a non-gendered adjective pressed into service as a verb, which is why it takes *buvo* and *bus* to change its tense rather than endings of its own.

examples.gloss: No, it is not allowed here.
Tomorrow it will be necessary to get up early.

rules.heading: Recognising an Impersonal Sentence
rules.statement: Three marks together identify one: there is **no nominative**, the verb or adjective stands in a form that **agrees with nothing**, and the person, if there is one, is in the **dative**. Where English inserts a dummy *it* — *it is cold*, *it is necessary*, *it hurts* — Lithuanian inserts nothing, and the absence is the construction.

examples.gloss: It was cold, so we stayed at home.
examples.note: the first clause impersonal, the second personal

vocabulary.gloss: to hurt, to ache (impersonal: + dat. and acc.)
vocabulary.notes: Impersonal: no subject; the sufferer is in the dative and the part in the accusative.

vocabulary.gloss: it is possible, one may (+ infinitive)

drills.stem: How is *It is cold today* said?
drills.explanation: There is no subject, so the adjective stands in its non-gendered form: *šalta*. A masculine *šaltas* would need something to agree with.
*lyja* has no subject and never will have one. English needs a dummy *it*; Lithuanian supplies nothing, and the absence is the construction.
*skaudėti* takes the sufferer in the dative and the part that hurts in the **accusative**: *galvą*. English makes the head the subject; Lithuanian makes it the object of a subjectless verb.

drills.stem: What is the difference between **Ji šalta** and **Jai šalta**?
options: None; the two are variants of one sentence.
The first says she is a cold person; the second says she feels cold.
The first is present and the second past.
drills.explanation: A nominative with an agreeing adjective describes what she **is**; a dative with the non-gendered form reports what she **feels**. Two letters carry the whole difference.
Adjectives in *-us* make their non-gendered form in **-u**: *įdomu*. *Filmas įdomus* would be the personal construction — the film *is* interesting — and *įdomiai* is the adverb.
The second has a nominative subject and a verb agreeing with it. The other three have no nominative anywhere, and their person, where there is one, stands in the dative.
*galima* is impersonal — *one may* — and is completed by an infinitive. *galiu* would say that **I** am able, which asks a different question.

options: Because the construction is impersonal: the sufferer goes into the dative and the part into the accusative, and no possessive is used.
Because the verb must be negated.
drills.explanation: *Man skauda galvą.* The possessive and the nominative both belong to the English sentence. Carrying them across is the single commonest error at the doctor's.

drills.stem: Which marks identify an impersonal sentence?
options: The verb or adjective agrees with nothing.
The person concerned, if named, stands in the dative.
drills.explanation: Negation has nothing to do with it: *Man šalta* and *Man nešalta* are both impersonal. The three real marks travel together, and any one of them is enough to suspect the construction.

drills.stem: **Man reikėjo dirbti, nes buvo šalta ir lijo.** How many nominatives does the sentence contain?
drills.explanation: None. *reikėjo*, *buvo šalta* and *lijo* are all impersonal, and *man* is a dative. A sentence of eight words with no subject anywhere is perfectly ordinary Lithuanian, and would be impossible in English without three separate dummy *it*s.

drills.title: Pas gydytoją
drills.passage:
– Laba diena. Kas jums yra?
– Man skauda galvą ir dantį. Vakar buvo šalta, o aš ilgai laukiau lauke.
– Ar jums sunku valgyti?
– Taip, sunku. Ir naktį buvo labai karšta — manau, kad sergu gripu.
– Suprantu. Jums reikės gerti vaistų ir ilsėtis. Dirbti negalima.
– O kada bus galima grįžti į darbą?
– Jeigu bus geriau, po savaitės. Bet jeigu skaudės ir toliau, ateikite dar kartą.
drills.translation: "Good afternoon. What is the matter with you?" — "My head and my tooth ache. Yesterday it was cold, and I waited outside for a long time." — "Is it difficult for you to eat?" — "Yes, it is. And in the night it was very hot — I think I have flu." — "I see. You will have to take medicine and rest. Working is not allowed." — "And when will it be possible to go back to work?" — "If you are better, in a week. But if it still hurts, come again."

glossary.Kas jums yra?: What is the matter with you?

questions.explanation: *Man skauda galvą ir dantį.* Both parts stand in the accusative, joined by *ir*, and the sufferer is in the dative.

questions.stem: Which expressions in the dialogue are **impersonal**?
questions.explanation: *sergu* is a perfectly personal first-person verb with *aš* understood (¶46). The other three have no subject at all: a non-gendered adjective, an impersonal of necessity, and one of prohibition.

questions.stem: After how many weeks may the patient go back to work, if he is better?
questions.explanation: *po savaitės* — after a week. *po* with the **genitive** is *after*, of time; with the instrumental it would have been *under* (¶75), and the ending is the whole of the difference.
